title: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)
word: the crow and the first verse
hook: Brahma visits the troubled poet and tells him the verse was meant
carry: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crow and the first verse. A krauncha bird, a hunter's arrow, and grief, shoka, pouring out as verse, shloka. Did something move you enough to write one line? Day four hundred ninety-four.

Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, but he can't let it go. He bathes, he sits, he tries to settle, and the verse keeps playing in his head, along with the guilt of having cursed someone. You know the feeling: a sentence you said today that you keep replaying at night. Then a visitor arrives. Not a wandering sage this time. Brahma himself, the creator, four-faced, the one the whole world comes from. And Valmiki, still lost in the bird's grief, can't stop saying the verse even in front of him.
screen: `REPLAYING IT AT NIGHT.` → `A VISITOR: BRAHMA.` → `STILL SAYING THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Brahma smiles, and settles it. Don't be troubled, he says. That verse came from me. It was meant to. Now tell the whole story of Rama, as Narada told it to you, in this same meter. What's hidden will be shown to you: what Rama did and said, what Sita did, what happened in private and in public. Not one word you speak in this poem will be false. And then the promise people still quote: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, so long will the story of Rama be told. Brahma disappears. Valmiki's students repeat the verse to each other in wonder. So Valmiki sits facing east, on a seat of sacred grass, sips water, and turns inward. And the story comes to him, the book says, in vision, all of it, laughter, talk, walks, everything, as clearly as if it were in front of him. He composes it. The tradition gives the count: twenty-four thousand verses, in what we now know as seven books. Then he needs someone to carry it. Two boys live in his hermitage, twins with beautiful voices, Kusha and Lava. He teaches them the whole poem by heart, and they sing it, at gatherings of sages and later in a king's court. Here's the turn: the twins are Rama's own sons, though Rama doesn't know them yet. The story will be sung to its own hero.
screen: `THE VERSE CAME FROM ME, SAYS BRAHMA.` · `NO WORD OF IT WILL BE FALSE.` · `AS LONG AS MOUNTAINS AND RIVERS.` · `TWO BOYS SING IT BY HEART.` · then, large: `TWENTY-FOUR THOUSAND VERSES.`

segments.voice: Sit facing whatever direction feels right, and let yourself be like Valmiki on his grass seat. Breathe in and out four times, slowly, counting the breaths like the four quarters of a verse. Then let the counting go. If a sentence from today keeps replaying, let it play once more, then set it beside you, the way Brahma set Valmiki's worry aside. Rest in what's left. The bell holds the time.
The crow and the first verse. Brahma tells Valmiki the verse was meant, and gives him the whole story of Rama to tell in that same meter.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE FIRST VERSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the crow and the first verse, the origin of poetry. Today, learn one short line of something you love by heart, a verse, a song, a saying, and say it once out loud. Day four hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: The Ramayana has long been passed on by heart and in song, and many Hindus recite or listen to its verses at home and in temples; the tradition of reciters traces itself back to Kusha and Lava singing Valmiki's poem.

original.note: Sanskrit śloka: verse, the epic meter of four quarters, eight syllables each.

trapdoor: what you thought: Valmiki sat down and wrote a book.
what it means: in the story, the poem is given, seen in vision, and passed on by voice.
what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 2–4 frame the epic: Brahma's commission, Valmiki's vision, and Kusha and Lava as its first reciters, kushilava, the old word for wandering bards.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 2 (Brahma's visit and promise)

notes: Brahma's promise (mountains and rivers) paraphrased from Bala Kanda 2; confirm.
Bala Kanda 4 gives 24,000 shlokas and speaks of six kandas plus the Uttara; the script says 'what we now know as seven books'. Confirm framing.
Kushilava as a word for bards and its link to Kusha and Lava is a traditional association; scholars debate the direction of the etymology. Confirm or drop from the trapdoor.
The 'four breaths like four quarters' practice is the script's own.
